Currently reading Use of Weapons by Banks, or book three of the Culture science fiction series.

I really liked Player of Games, and while for the most part I liked Consider Phlebas, it had the problem of being too preachy, and too "alien for the sake of being alien" occasionally. And it was that last part that kept me from reading Use of Weapons. And for that, I am sorry.

Use of Weapons is really well structured, it has one major story arc playing out in real time, while it uses memories/flashbacks to construct a relevant picture of the characters involved. Because it has been a few years since I read Player of Games, I didn't realise how much I missed the AI in the Culture. And one thing it does have going for it is that while I was annoyed at some of the "world building" in Consider Plebas, that has not been the case so far, and has been part of the natural progression through Player of Games. It really is nice to see an author improve over the course of a couple of novels, especially when the first was strong. Though in retrospect, that seems to be a trait of all my favourite authors. Yes, it is not a happy-go-lucky space romp, nor should it be due to the topics delved into, so it is meant to be rougher emotionally, and so far, a very good read.
Now I really want to read it. After finishing it, you still consider it to be too preachy or did the narrative somehow require it to be so?

Consider Plebas is an odd beast, because of the arc of the central character, and how it set up the "world" of the Culture. "narrative somehow require it to be so" is actually, upon reflection, the best way to describe it.

Both Player of Games, and Use of Weapons (so far), have not fallen into the same trap, where the central characters, and the conflicts they inhabit are much more fluid, more forgiving to the different parties involved, and even draped in the academic game theory approach in PoG, more intimate, due to the characters themselves, and the trials they face. And oddly enough, the AI that have been some of the best characters in all three books so far, who have been more prominent in the latter two.

Anyway, it all comes down to you, and your preferences in (science) fiction. I will be the first to admit that the Culture series may not for everyone. A lot of people recommend to read Player of Games first, I made a conscious decision to read a "weaker" novel in the series as the start, for both the sake of completeness, and chronological order. I was fairly sure of myself at least reading the first two, no matter the outcome.

And that was because of two reasons. An author I respected said "If you've never read any of his books, read one of his books. Then read another. Even the bad ones were good, and the good ones were astonishing." The wikipedia summary had just enough to pique my interest on different aspects in science fiction "The stories center on the Culture, a utopian society of humanoids, aliens, and very advanced artificial intelligences living in semi-anarchist habitats spread across the post-material-scarcity Milky Way galaxy. The main theme of the novels is the dilemmas that an idealistic hyperpower faces in dealing with civilisations that do not share its ideals, and whose behaviour it sometimes finds repulsive. In some of the stories, action takes place mainly in non-Culture environments, and the leading characters are often on the fringes of, or non-members of, the Culture, sometimes acting as agents of Culture plans to civilise the galaxy."
